source_refs.note: Book p. 102-103: 6.6.1 A > G if a ≠ b, A = G if a = b; Example 17 (three G.M.s between 2 and 1/2, four values of r) and the Note after it

blocks.text:
If \(A\) and \(G\) are respectively A.M. and G.M. between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) i.e.,
\[A = \dfrac{a+b}{2}\ \text{ and }\ G = \sqrt{ab},\]
then

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here \(a\) and \(b\) are positive and \(G\) is the positive G.M. \(\sqrt{ab}\) (with \(-\sqrt{ab}\) the comparison would be trivial). The result says: the A.M. of two different positive numbers is always bigger than their G.M.; they are equal only when the two numbers are equal. You will prove it in Exercise 6.6, Question 3.

blocks.caption: A.M. and G.M. of some positive numbers (our illustration)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: The farther apart \(a\) and \(b\) are, the bigger the gap \(A - G\) (compare rows 1 and 2 above). If a question gives \(A\) and \(G\) of two numbers, use \(a + b = 2A\) and \(ab = G^{2}\), and the numbers are the roots of \(x^{2} - 2Ax + G^{2} = 0\).

blocks.title: Example 17
steps:
Given: the two numbers \(2\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\).
To find: three G.M.s \(G_1, G_2, G_3\) between them.
Method: \(2, G_1, G_2, G_3, \frac{1}{2}\) must be a G.P. of 5 terms. Use the general term \(a_n = a_1r^{n-1}\) with the last term to find \(r\); then \(G_1 = a_1r\), \(G_2 = a_1r^{2}\), \(G_3 = a_1r^{3}\).

Step 1: Write the G.P. and read off the data
\[2,\ G_1,\ G_2,\ G_3,\ \tfrac{1}{2}\]
\[a_1 = 2,\quad a_5 = \tfrac{1}{2},\quad n = 5\]
Why: three means plus the two given numbers make \(3 + 2 = 5\) terms, and \(\frac{1}{2}\) is the 5th term.

Step 2: Use the general term
\[a_n = a_1r^{n-1}\]
\[a_5 = a_1r^{5-1}\]
\[a_5 = a_1r^{4} \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: the only unknown in the G.P. is \(r\); the general term links \(r\) to the known first and last terms.

Step 3: Substitute \(a_5\) and \(a_1\) in (i)
\[\tfrac{1}{2} = 2r^{4}\]
\[r^{4} = \tfrac{1}{4} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: dividing both sides by 2 isolates \(r^{4}\).

Step 4: Take the square root of (ii)
\[r^{2} = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}\]
Why: \(r^{4} = (r^{2})^{2}\), so \(r^{2}\) is a square root of \(\frac{1}{4}\), and a number has two square roots.

Step 5: Find \(r\) in both cases
\[r^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow r = \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
\[r^{2} = -\tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{i^{2}}{2}\]
\[\Rightarrow r = \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,i\]
Why: using \(-1 = i^{2}\) turns the negative case into a perfect square of \(\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\). So there are four values of \(r\).

Step 7: \(r = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\[G_1 = 2\left(\tfrac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = -\sqrt{2}\]
\[G_2 = 2\left(\tfrac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2} = 1\]
\[G_3 = 2\left(\tfrac{-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{3} = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: an even power removes the minus sign; an odd power keeps it.

Step 8: \(r = \frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\)
\[G_1 = 2\left(\tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \sqrt{2}\,i\]
\[G_2 = 2\left(\tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2} = -1\]
\[G_3 = 2\left(\tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{3} = -\tfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(i^{2} = -1\) and \(i^{3} = -i\). The book writes \(G_1\) as \(\sqrt{2}i\); it means \(\sqrt{2}\) times \(i\), not \(\sqrt{2i}\).

Check:
For \(r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) the G.P. is \(2, \sqrt{2}, 1, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{2}\); each term is the one before it times \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).
For every \(r\) found, \(r^{4} = \frac{1}{4}\) (for example \(\left(\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{4} = \frac{i^{4}}{4} = \frac{1}{4}\)), so the 5th term is \(2 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}\) every time.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The real values of \(r\) are usually taken but here other cases are considered to widen the outlook of the students.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: If a question says 'insert real geometric means', give only the real values of \(r\) (here \(r = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)). Unless told otherwise, the case \(r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) with all means positive is the usual answer.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. For positive \(a, b\): \(A = \frac{a+b}{2}\), \(G = \sqrt{ab}\).
2. \(A > G\) when \(a \ne b\); \(A = G\) when \(a = b\).
3. To insert \(n\) G.M.s, find \(r\) from (last term) \(= a_1r^{n+1}\), then \(G_k = a_1r^{k}\).
4. \(r^{4} = \frac{1}{4}\) has four solutions \(\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \pm\frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\); real means use the real ones.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using \(n = 3\) in Example 17: the G.P. has 5 terms, so \(a_5 = a_1r^{4}\).
2. From \(r^{4} = \frac{1}{4}\) writing only \(r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\): \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) also works.
3. Reading \(\sqrt{2}i\) as \(\sqrt{2i}\): it is \(\sqrt{2}\times i\).
4. Getting \(G_2 = 1\) for \(r = \frac{i}{\sqrt{2}}\): \(i^{2} = -1\), so \(G_2 = -1\).
